blocks.body:
A friend claims his spinner lands on red a quarter of the time. You spin it 20 times and get 9 reds, where you would expect 5. Is the spinner unfair, or was this just chance? Chance can produce almost anything, so the question has to be made sharper: if the friend's claim were true, how unusual would 9 or more reds be?

That is the logic of a hypothesis test. Assume a default claim, work out what data it predicts, and see whether the actual data fit. It uses the sampling distributions of [[confidence-intervals]] and the binomial and normal models of [[distributions]].

blocks.title: The ingredients
blocks.body:
A test has four parts.

1. The null hypothesis $H_0$: the default claim, a precise statement about a parameter, such as $p = 0.25$. It is what we assume while computing probabilities.
2. The alternative hypothesis $H_1$: what we suspect instead. It is one-sided ($p > 0.25$, or $p < 0.25$) or two-sided ($p \ne 0.25$). It must be chosen before looking at the data, from the question being asked.
3. A test statistic $T$: a number computed from the data whose distribution under $H_0$ is known, here the number $X$ of reds, which is binomial $B(20, 0.25)$ if $H_0$ holds.
4. A decision rule, fixed in advance through the significance level $\alpha$, commonly $0.05$.

The test can end in only two ways: reject $H_0$ (the data are evidence for $H_1$), or fail to reject $H_0$ (the data are consistent with $H_0$). Failing to reject is not proof that $H_0$ is true; it may just mean the sample was too small to see a difference.

blocks.title: p-value
blocks.body:
The p-value of an observed statistic $t_{\text{obs}}$ is the probability, computed assuming $H_0$ is true, of obtaining a value of the test statistic at least as extreme as $t_{\text{obs}}$, where "extreme" means in the direction of $H_1$. We reject $H_0$ at level $\alpha$ when the p-value is at most $\alpha$.

A small p-value means the data would be rare if $H_0$ were true. It is not the probability that $H_0$ is true.

blocks.title: The spinner, step by step
blocks.body:
Take $H_0: p = 0.25$ and $H_1: p > 0.25$ at the 5% level. Assuming the spins are independent, each with the same chance of red, under $H_0$ we have $X \sim B(20, 0.25)$, and we observed $X = 9$. Large values favour $H_1$, so
$$\text{p-value} = P(X \ge 9) = \sum_{k=9}^{20}\binom{20}{k}(0.25)^k(0.75)^{20-k} \approx 0.0409.$$
This is below $0.05$, so we reject $H_0$: there is evidence at the 5% level that the spinner lands on red more than a quarter of the time.

An equivalent view uses a critical region, the set of values of $T$ that lead to rejection. Here $P(X\ge 8) \approx 0.102$ and $P(X \ge 9) \approx 0.041$, so the critical region at the 5% level is $X \ge 9$, and the observed $9$ lies in it. Because $X$ is discrete, the actual probability of rejecting a true $H_0$ is $0.041$, a little below the nominal 5%.

For a two-sided alternative $p \ne 0.25$ we would put about $\alpha/2$ in each tail, or double the smaller one-tailed probability to get the p-value.

blocks.title: Two kinds of error
blocks.body:
The decision can go wrong in two ways.

- Type I error: rejecting $H_0$ when it is true. Its probability is the size of the test, at most $\alpha$.
- Type II error: failing to reject $H_0$ when it is false. Its probability is called $\beta$, and it depends on the true value of the parameter.

The power of the test is $1-\beta$, the probability of correctly rejecting a false $H_0$. For the spinner test with critical region $X \ge 9$, if the true probability of red is $p = 0.4$, then $X \sim B(20, 0.4)$ and the power is $P(X\ge 9) \approx 0.404$. Even a fairly strong bias is missed more often than not with only 20 spins.

The two errors pull against each other: shrinking the critical region lowers $\alpha$ but raises $\beta$. The only way to reduce both is more data. Choosing $\alpha$ is a judgement about which mistake is costlier, which is why a courtroom (where $H_0$ is "innocent") demands strong evidence.

blocks.title: Tests based on the normal distribution
blocks.body:
When the test statistic is approximately normal, the p-value comes from the standard normal table. For a mean, with known $\sigma$ and $H_0: \mu = \mu_0$,
$$Z = \frac{\bar X - \mu_0}{\sigma/\sqrt n}$$
is exactly $N(0,1)$ under $H_0$ if the population is normal, and approximately so for large $n$ by the central limit theorem. For a proportion with $H_0: p = p_0$ we use
$$Z = \frac{\hat p - p_0}{\sqrt{p_0(1-p_0)/n}},$$
with the null value $p_0$ in the standard error, because the probabilities are computed assuming $H_0$. Assumptions in both cases: a random sample, independent observations, and a large enough sample for the normal approximation ($np_0$ and $n(1-p_0)$ at least about 10).

At the 5% level the two-sided critical values are $\pm 1.96$, and the one-sided critical value is $1.645$.

There is a direct link with confidence intervals: a two-sided test at level $\alpha$ rejects $\mu = \mu_0$ exactly when $\mu_0$ lies outside the level $1-\alpha$ interval $\bar x \pm z^*\sigma/\sqrt n$, because both statements say $|\bar x - \mu_0| > z^*\sigma/\sqrt n$.

blocks.title: A filling machine
blocks.body: A machine fills bottles with a nominal 500 ml. The fill volume is normal with standard deviation 4 ml. A made-up random sample of 25 bottles has mean $498.2$ ml. Test at the 5% level whether the machine's mean has drifted from 500 ml, and find the power of this test if the true mean is 498 ml.
blocks.solution:
We test $H_0: \mu = 500$ against $H_1: \mu \ne 500$; drift in either direction matters. The standard error is $4/\sqrt{25} = 0.8$, so
$$z = \frac{498.2 - 500}{0.8} = -2.25.$$
The two-sided p-value is $2P(Z \le -2.25) \approx 0.0244 < 0.05$, so we reject $H_0$: there is evidence the machine has drifted.

The test rejects when $\bar x$ is outside $500 \pm 1.96\times 0.8$, that is below $498.432$ or above $501.568$. If $\mu = 498$, then $\bar X \sim N(498, 0.8^2)$ and
$$\text{power} = P(\bar X < 498.432) + P(\bar X > 501.568) \approx 0.705.$$
A drift of 2 ml is caught about 70% of the time with samples of 25.

blocks.title: Is there a majority?
blocks.body: In a made-up poll 232 of 400 randomly chosen voters support a proposal. Test $H_0: p = 0.5$ against $H_1: p > 0.5$.
blocks.solution:
Under $H_0$ the standard error is $\sqrt{0.5\times 0.5/400} = 0.025$, and $\hat p = 0.58$, so
$$z = \frac{0.58-0.5}{0.025} = 3.2, \qquad \text{p-value} = P(Z \ge 3.2) \approx 0.0007.$$
The conditions hold: the voters are a random sample from a large population, and $np_0 = n(1-p_0) = 200 \ge 10$. This is strong evidence of majority support. It agrees with the 95% confidence interval $(0.532, 0.628)$ found in [[confidence-intervals]], which lies entirely above $0.5$.

blocks.title: Tasting tea
blocks.body: A taster claims she can tell whether milk was poured into a cup before or after the tea. She is given 8 cups, told that exactly 4 had milk first, and asked to pick those 4. Under $H_0$ (she is guessing) all choices are equally likely. Find the p-value if she identifies all 4 correctly, and if she gets exactly 3 right.
blocks.solution:
There are $\binom84 = 70$ equally likely ways to choose 4 cups. Exactly one of them is entirely correct, so if she gets all 4 right the p-value is $1/70 \approx 0.0143$, significant at the 5% level.

To get exactly 3 right she must choose 3 of the 4 milk-first cups and 1 of the other 4, which can be done in $\binom43\binom41 = 16$ ways. The p-value for "at least 3 right" is $(16+1)/70 \approx 0.243$: three out of four is entirely consistent with guessing. Notice that this design could never give a p-value below $0.05$ unless she is perfect; a test with too little data has low power by construction.

blocks.title: Tests without a normal model
blocks.body:
Sometimes we cannot assume a normal population. The sign test needs almost nothing. Suppose 10 people each try two diets, and 8 of them lose more weight on diet A. Under $H_0$ (the diets are equally good, and ties do not occur) each person, independently of the others, is equally likely to favour either diet, so the number favouring A is $B(10, 0.5)$. Then
$$P(X \ge 8) = \frac{\binom{10}{8}+\binom{10}{9}+\binom{10}{10}}{2^{10}} = \frac{56}{1024} \approx 0.0547,$$
and the two-sided p-value is $0.109$. The evidence is suggestive but not significant at the 5% level. Such non-parametric tests trade some power for robustness; refinements such as the Wilcoxon signed-rank test also use the sizes of the differences.

blocks.title: Going further: the best test
blocks.body: Why use $\bar X$ or $X$ as the test statistic rather than something else? For two simple hypotheses, each specifying the distribution completely, there is a definitive answer. Write $f_0$ and $f_1$ for the density or mass function of the data under $H_0$ and $H_1$. A test can be described by a function $\phi(x)\in[0,1]$, the probability of rejecting when the data are $x$; its size is $\operatorname{E}_0[\phi]$ and its power is $\operatorname{E}_1[\phi]$.

blocks.title: Neyman-Pearson lemma
blocks.body: Let $k \ge 0$ and let $\phi^*$ be a test that rejects when $f_1(x) > k f_0(x)$ and does not reject when $f_1(x) < k f_0(x)$, with size $\operatorname{E}_0[\phi^*] = \alpha$. Then every test $\phi$ with size $\operatorname{E}_0[\phi] \le \alpha$ has power $\operatorname{E}_1[\phi] \le \operatorname{E}_1[\phi^*]$.

At each point $x$, the product $(\phi^*(x)-\phi(x))(f_1(x) - k f_0(x))$ is non-negative. Indeed, where $f_1 > kf_0$ we have $\phi^* = 1 \ge \phi$; where $f_1 < kf_0$ we have $\phi^* = 0 \le \phi$; and where $f_1 = kf_0$ the second factor is $0$. Summing or integrating over all $x$,
$$\operatorname{E}_1[\phi^*] - \operatorname{E}_1[\phi] \ge k\big(\operatorname{E}_0[\phi^*] - \operatorname{E}_0[\phi]\big) = k\big(\alpha - \operatorname{E}_0[\phi]\big) \ge 0.$$

blocks.title: What the lemma says in practice
blocks.body: The most powerful test rejects when the likelihood ratio $f_1/f_0$ is large. For a normal sample with known $\sigma$ and $H_1: \mu = \mu_1 > \mu_0$, the ratio is an increasing function of $\bar x$, so "reject when $\bar x$ is large" is the most powerful test, and since it does not depend on which $\mu_1 > \mu_0$ was chosen, it is uniformly most powerful against $\mu > \mu_0$. For composite hypotheses the same idea gives the likelihood-ratio test, which compares maximised likelihoods and connects testing to [[point-estimation]].

- The p-value is not the probability that $H_0$ is true, nor the probability that the result was "due to chance". It is a probability about data, computed assuming $H_0$.
- Statistical significance is not practical importance. With a huge sample, a difference too small to matter becomes significant.
- Not rejecting $H_0$ does not prove it; the test may simply have low power.
- Choosing a one-sided alternative after seeing which way the data point halves the p-value dishonestly.
- Running many tests and reporting the significant ones guarantees false discoveries: with 20 independent true nulls at the 5% level, the chance of at least one rejection is $1 - 0.95^{20} \approx 0.64$.
- Every test has assumptions (random sampling, independence, a model for the statistic). A p-value computed under false assumptions means little.

Tests for means when $\sigma$ is unknown, and for comparing several means at once, are in [[t-tests]]. Tests for counts in categories and for independence in two-way tables are in [[chi-square-tests]]. Every two-sided test corresponds to a confidence interval, as in [[confidence-intervals]]. Sequential testing, where data arrive one at a time, leads to [[martingales]].

1. A die is thrown 30 times and shows a six 9 times. Test at the 5% level whether it shows six more often than $1/6$ of the time, using the binomial distribution.
2. For the spinner test with critical region $X \ge 9$ out of 20, find the probability of a Type II error if in fact $p = 0.5$.
3. A two-sided z-test gives $z = 1.8$. Find the p-value. Would a one-sided test in the direction of the data reject at the 5% level? Why is it wrong to decide this after seeing $z$?
4. Explain, with an example, why a 99% confidence interval excluding $\mu_0$ implies that the two-sided test of $\mu = \mu_0$ rejects at the 1% level.
